newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Kerry on lookout for acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kerry on lookout for acquisitions.

text.p: After successfully swallowing a number of major companies in recent years, Irish food company Kerry Group Plc says it is again on the lookout for acquisitions.

"There is huge potential for us across international markets, both in our existing consumer food businesses and in the global ingredients markets," Frank Hayes, director of corporate affairs at Kerry, told Reuters in an interview.

Kerry acquired DCA Food Industries Inc from Allied Domecq in November 1994 for $402 million and purchased Mattesson Walls from Unilever unit Van den Bergh Foods Ltd for an undisclosed sum in July 1994.

Now that it has completed the integration of both companies, as well as absorbing European fruit ingredients firm Ciprial, Kerry plans to grow those businesses and explore acquisition opportunities in international growth markets.
"In terms of future developments, we will continue to look at any opportunities that arise in our chosen niches," Hayes said.

Hayes said the group had nothing specific in mind right now but the acquisition of the remaining 50 percent equity in the Solutech DCA joint venture last year has given it a toehold in the Asia-Pacific region.

"Having an actual manufacturing presence in Australia and having a dedicated team working there is an important foothold for us. Looking to the future development of our ingredients business, a lot of our major customers are expanding in those markets and it's inevitable that there will be opportunities for us in pursuit of them," he said.
But he said Kerry was just beginning to focus on and analyse market opportunities in the area and had no specific plans on how to proceed.
He said the company would also look at all relevant opportunities that arose for its consumer foods business in Europe.

Hayes said the company was pleased with the performance of the business in the first part of this year and hopeful of a good result for the year as a whole while the raw material price inflation seen in 1996 had been largely overcome.
"Prices have now normalised and are back to 1995 levels," Hayes said.

Earlier, Kerry reported an 18.6 percent rise in 1996 pre-tax profit to 51.2 million Irish pounds despite difficult trading conditions caused by the abnormally high raw material costs across international markets.
All core businesses performed well with operating profit margins increasing to 7.35 percent from 7.15 percent.
Kerry's food ingredients division reported a 14 percent rise in sales while trading profits rose by 7.3 percent to 64.9 million pounds against a background of significant raw material cost inflation.
Businesses acquired in 1996, including Ciprial which was acquired for 54 million Irish pounds last year, contributed an estimated operating profit of around 4.0 million punts, Kerry said.

The consumer foods business recorded an 8.7 percent rise in operating profits to 24.5 million Irish pounds and now accounts for 27 percent of group operating profits while food ingredients account for 72 percent.
In geographic terms, sales outside Ireland now represent 78 percent of group revenue with 41.6 percent of turnover in Europe and 35.3 percent in North America.
The group's smallest division, its agribusiness unit, reported a drop in operating profit to 2.2 million Irish pounds from 1.2 million in 1995.
